claims.text: Controlled thermal-gradient annealing of high-entropy-alloy intermediate layers will enhance heat-transfer capability while preserving or improving structural integrity.
Conventionally processed high-entropy-alloy intermediate layers have an equiaxed grain structure.
Conventionally processed high-entropy-alloy intermediate layers have moderate thermal conductivity and acceptable mechanical strength.
Controlled thermal-gradient annealing will induce directional grain alignment and elongated, columnar grains.
Temperatures above 700°C combined with high cyclic mechanical loading are representative of plasma-facing reactor environments.
Directional grain boundaries and elongated columnar grains act as continuous channels for heat transport.
Interlocking among the engineered grains supports mechanical integrity.
An imposed thermal gradient during annealing drives preferential grain growth along the gradient.
Preferential grain growth aligns grain boundaries into continuous pathways.
Aligned grain-boundary pathways provide more efficient heat conduction.
Retained interlocking grain structures maintain or improve mechanical strength under extreme thermal and mechanical stresses.
Thermal-gradient-annealed layers will have higher measured thermal conductivity than as-fabricated layers.
Thermal-gradient-annealed layers will maintain or improve mechanical strength under high temperature and cyclic loading compared with as-fabricated layers.
The beneficial effect depends on precise control of the thermal gradient.
A nonoptimized thermal treatment may cause excessive grain growth that compromises mechanical properties.
The quantitative thermal-conductivity improvement and strength tradeoff under actual reactor conditions remain undetermined.
